HyperSkill: Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO via Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library Evolution

Haoran Luo, Shangkai Lin, Jinyang Wu, Xinliang Zhou, Luu Anh Tuan Email: haoran.luo@ntu.edu.sg, xinliang.zhou@stanford.edu, anhtuan.luu@ntu.edu.sg Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Tsinghua University Stanford University VinUniversity
Abstract

Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available1.

$\dagger$$\dagger$footnotetext: Project Lead. ∗*Corresponding Authors. 1https://github.com/LHRLAB/HyperSkill

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning is now the main way to improve the reasoning of large language models (LLMs), with group-relative policy optimisation (GRPO) [39, 52, 55] used to train systems in math, search, and tool use [14, 49, 18, 10]. However, it is still hard to keep improving an agent as it moves to omnimodal tasks such as web search, long-document reasoning, and audio-video question answering [45, 48, 58, 23], without a per-domain cost of updating its backbone.

Existing methods follow two main lines. The mainstream parameter-space recipe applies gradient updates to the backbone, yielding capable but costly systems [14, 49, 18, 10]. A growing training-free line keeps the backbone frozen and grows an external textual experience store across rollouts, retrieved in-context at inference [2, 1, 3, 50, 41, 44].

Both lines have limits. On the parameter side (Figure 1), gradient updates remain expensive at frontier scale [14], every new task risks catastrophic forgetting [54], and improvement is buried in opaque weight deltas with no auditable trace of which patterns the agent has internalised. On the training-free side, three failure modes recur (Figure 2): (i) comparison is at the trajectory level [2, 1], so every divergent step is fused into one lesson; (ii) candidates are admitted by co-occurrence with successful rollouts [2, 3, 50], so the library keeps patterns that track reward but do not fix the failure; (iii) skills are stored as dictionaries or uniform-quality lists, which cannot express that several skills must act jointly or give a per-skill quality signal. Hypergraph retrieval [26, 11, 53] links several entities in one hyperedge, but it targets static factual knowledge bases rather than self-evolving skill libraries.

To close all three gaps, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework whose policy is an external Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library: atomic skills are advantage-bearing nodes, joint compositions are hyperedges, and the library is the optimisation target. C1 (training-time distillation) handles (i) and (ii): it admits a step-level candidate only after a counterfactual test (“would the failed trajectory have succeeded had the agent known this skill?”) and learns a protocol skill from failures. C2 (gated hypergraph retrieval) handles (iii): an advantage-weighted retriever [20, 13, 15] ranks hyperedge-linked skills [26, 11, 25] behind a gate with zero-skill fallback. C3 (execution protocol) makes the frozen backbone call its tools correctly and then commit to a final answer.

We validate this design across 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks [45, 4, 27, 16]: HyperSkill is best or tied on all 11 without updating a parameter, and lifts the average F1 from 29.029.0 for the strongest baseline, XSkill [17], to 42.042.0 (+13.0+13.0, 44.9%44.9\% relative). Each component matters: removing C1, C2 or C3 alone lowers the average F1 by 2.52.5, 4.24.2 and 10.410.4 points, respectively.

2 Related Work

Omnimodal LLMs and reinforcement learning. Modern backbones fuse text, image, video, and audio into a single policy [35, 24, 36, 31, 48, 58, 23], and group-relative policy optimisation [39, 52, 55] trains reasoners [14, 32] and search and tool agents [18, 10, 25], while reflection-style agents [51, 40, 28] act through prompting on web and OS benchmarks [57, 45, 47]. The RL-trained ones still pay for backbone gradient updates and inherit the forgetting and opacity problems motivating this work. Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO keeps the backbone frozen and redirects a normalised reward advantage from the gradient onto an external Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library that acts as the policy, so each improvement is a readable library edit rather than an opaque weight delta.

Training-free experience self-evolution. TrainingFreeGRPO [2] replaces the gradient with an LLM-curated experience pool, skill-centric agents [1, 3, 50, 41, 44] grow flat dictionaries or frontier sets, and memory [33, 6, 34] with graph and hypergraph RAG [9, 15, 26, 11] supplies the retrievable side. Most of them compare whole trajectories and keep flat skills with no per-item quality for ranking; HyperSkill instead distils individual steps and ranks skills by advantage in a hypergraph.

3 Methodology: HyperSkill

Problem Formulation. Unlike the methods of Table 1, HyperSkill couples a per-skill quality signal with explicit multi-skill compositions in a weighted skill hypergraph. Formally, let πθ\pi_{\theta} be a frozen omnimodal backbone whose parameters θ\theta are never updated, and let 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} and 𝒟test\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} be train and test sets of triples (q,a∗,m)(q,a^{*},m), in which each query qq carries a gold answer a∗a^{*} and a modality tag m∈ℳ={text,image,pdf,video,audio}m\!\in\!\mathcal{M}\!=\!\{\text{text},\text{image},\text{pdf},\text{video},\text{audio}\}. We seek a weighted skill hypergraph ℋ=(𝒱,ℰ,w)\mathcal{H}\!=\!(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},w) in which every node vi∈𝒱v_{i}\!\in\!\mathcal{V} carries a name, a description and an advantage ui∈[−1,1]u_{i}\!\in\![-1,1], and every hyperedge ej∈ℰe_{j}\!\in\!\mathcal{E} groups |ej|≥2|e_{j}|\!\geq\!2 nodes into a joint composition with weight w⁡(ej)w(e_{j}). We also seek a retriever ℛ:(q,m,ℋ)→𝒮q⊂𝒱\mathcal{R}\!:\!(q,m,\mathcal{H})\!\to\!\mathcal{S}_{q}\!\subset\!\mathcal{V} under which the skill-augmented policy improves on its skill-free version, while a hypergraph update 𝒰\mathcal{U} replaces the gradient step in every round tt:

(ℋ⋆,ℛ⋆)=argmaxℋ,ℛ𝔼(q,a∗,m)∼𝒟[r(πθ(⋅∣q,m,ℛ(q,m,ℋ));a∗)],ℋt+1=𝒰(ℋt;ℬt),\bigl(\mathcal{H}^{\star},\,\mathcal{R}^{\star}\bigr)\;=\;\arg\!\max_{\mathcal{H},\,\mathcal{R}}\;\mathbb{E}_{(q,a^{*},m)\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\Bigl[\,r\bigl(\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!q,m,\mathcal{R}(q,m,\mathcal{H}))\,;\,a^{*}\,\bigr)\,\Bigr]\,,\quad\mathcal{H}_{t+1}\!=\!\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})\,, (1)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the task distribution (𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} in training, 𝒟test\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} at evaluation), ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} the round-tt training batch and rr the token-level F1F_{1} reward against a∗a^{*}. Unlike GRPO, the optimisation variable is the pair (ℋ,ℛ)(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{R}) rather than θ\theta: gradient updates are replaced by an iterative, auditable rewrite of the library. C1 (§3.1) handles gaps (i) and (ii), C2 (§3.2) handles gap (iii), and C3 (§3.3) fixes execution failures of the frozen backbone; Figure 3 gives an overview of how C1 and C2 build, evolve and query the library.

3.1 C1: Training-Time Skill Distillation

To address (i) and (ii), we move admission from trajectories to steps and route every candidate through a counterfactual probe before insertion, so that a skill enters 𝒱\mathcal{V} only if the frozen backbone judges it to salvage a failure of its own question rather than merely co-occurring with a success.

Contrastive Step Alignment. For every question q∈ℬtq\!\in\!\mathcal{B}_{t} we draw a group of nn skill-augmented rollouts {o(ℓ)}ℓ=1n∼πθ(⋅∣q,m,ℛ(q,m,ℋt))\{o^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell=1}^{n}\!\sim\!\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!q,m,\mathcal{R}(q,m,\mathcal{H}_{t})) under the frozen backbone, score each by the token-level F1F_{1} reward, and split the group at threshold ρ=0.5\rho\!=\!0.5 into a success bucket 𝒪q+\mathcal{O}_{q}^{+} and a failure bucket 𝒪q−\mathcal{O}_{q}^{-}. A regex decomposer Ψ\Psi (zero LLM cost) slices every rollout into a step sequence Ψ⁡(o)=(s1,…,sTo)\Psi(o)\!=\!(s_{1},\dots,s_{T_{o}}), after which an LLM aligner Φ\Phi matches steps that solve the same sub-goal across the two buckets and harvests each divergent atomic skill that successes show but failures miss:

𝒱~q=Φ⁡({Ψ⁡(o(ℓ)):r⁡(o(ℓ),a∗)≥ρ}ℓ=1n,{Ψ⁡(o(ℓ)):r⁡(o(ℓ),a∗)<ρ}ℓ=1n),\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}\;=\;\Phi\!\Bigl(\,\bigl\{\,\Psi(o^{(\ell)})\!:\!r(o^{(\ell)};a^{*})\!\geq\!\rho\,\bigr\}_{\ell=1}^{n}\,,\;\;\bigl\{\,\Psi(o^{(\ell)})\!:\!r(o^{(\ell)};a^{*})\!<\!\rho\,\bigr\}_{\ell=1}^{n}\,\Bigr), (2)

where each candidate v~∈𝒱~q\widetilde{v}\!\in\!\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q} is a (name, description) pair, and the aligner may also name a recipe e~⊂𝒱~q\widetilde{e}\!\subset\!\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q} of candidates that the successes used jointly, which becomes a hyperedge once at least two of its members are admitted. The contrast is thus localised to the divergence point of the two buckets, so noisy steps of successful rollouts are less likely to enter the harvested skill or recipe.

Counterfactual Verification. Step alignment alone still admits skills that merely correlate with success; we therefore pair each candidate with a list 𝒫q\mathcal{P}_{q} of at most KK failure probes o−∈𝒪q−o^{-}\!\in\!\mathcal{O}_{q}^{-} of its own question and ask the same frozen πθ\pi_{\theta} a binary counterfactual probe [42, 28, 40]: “had the agent known v~\widetilde{v}, would o−o^{-} likely have produced a∗a^{*}?”. Only when a strict majority of the probes return YES is the candidate admitted into the round-tt skill increment, and a deterministic identifier sid⁡(v~)=md5⁡(name⁡(v~))\mathrm{sid}(\widetilde{v})\!=\!\mathrm{md5}(\mathrm{name}(\widetilde{v})) deduplicates it against the current library 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} by skill name:

𝒱tnew={v~∈𝒱~q:1|𝒫q|∑o−∈𝒫q[πθ(⋅∣v~,q,a∗,o−)=YES]>12},|𝒫q|≤K=2.\mathcal{V}_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}\;=\;\Bigl\{\;\widetilde{v}\!\in\!\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}\;:\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{q}|}\!\sum_{o^{-}\in\mathcal{P}_{q}}\!\mathbf{1}\!\bigl[\,\pi_{\theta}\!\bigl(\,\cdot\!\mid\!\widetilde{v},\,q,\,a^{*},\,o^{-}\bigr)\!=\!\mathrm{YES}\,\bigr]\;>\;\tfrac{1}{2}\;\;\Bigr\}\,,\qquad|\mathcal{P}_{q}|\!\leq\!K\!=\!2. (3)

The admitted increment 𝒱tnew\mathcal{V}_{t}^{\mathrm{new}} and its recipes ℰtrec\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\mathrm{rec}} feed the hypergraph evolution of C2 (§3.2).

Protocol Skill and Answer Form. A frozen backbone often breaks the tool or answer format, not the task. C1 therefore sorts every training rollout that ends without an answer into four failure types: malformed tool call, call beyond the budget, call without tools, and no <answer> tag. Each tool-related type seen in at least 22 rollouts adds fixed instruction lines, filled with the dataset’s tool tags and budget, to a protocol skill. Its last line fixes the answer form: the integer without \boxed{} on math, else a short answer or, per dataset, a form derived from the training gold answers (option letter, phrase or sentence, plus an abstention line). The protocol skill is not a node of ℋ\mathcal{H} (App. A).

Proposition 1. Counterfactual distillation favours failure-rescuing skills over co-occurring ones.

Proof.

We provide experimental results in §4.3 and §4.4 and proofs in Appendix B.1. ∎

3.2 C2: Hypergraph Evolution and Gated Retrieval

To address (iii), the survivors of C1 form a weighted hypergraph ℋ=(𝒱,ℰ,w)\mathcal{H}\!=\!(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},w). During training, rollout rewards are recycled, with no extra LLM call, into a per-node advantage and per-edge weights; at test time, with the library frozen, C2 ranks, gates and injects skills for every question.

Hypergraph Index and Advantage EMA Update. Each admitted skill viv_{i} is embedded by a frozen text encoder ff and stored with its advantage uiu_{i} in a dual key-value/vector-database (KV/VDB) index; admitted recipes and skill sets retrieved together for high-reward questions become hyperedges ej⊂𝒱e_{j}\!\subset\!\mathcal{V} with |ej|≥2|e_{j}|\!\geq\!2. After every batch, the batch-normalised mean reward of each question qq is broadcast to its retrieved skills 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}, and an exponential moving average with rate η\eta updates their advantages uiu_{i}:

A^q=tanh⁡(r¯q−r¯ℬtσr,ℬt+ϵ),ui←clip[−1,1]​((−η)​ui+η​A^q)​∀vi∈𝒮q,\hat{A}_{q}\;=\;\tanh\!\Bigl(\,\tfrac{\bar{r}_{q}\,-\,\bar{r}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}}{\sigma_{r,\mathcal{B}_{t}}\,+\,\epsilon}\,\Bigr)\,,\quad u_{i}\;\leftarrow\;\mathrm{clip}_{[-1,1]}\!\bigl(\,(1\!-\!\eta)\,u_{i}\,+\,\eta\,\hat{A}_{q}\,\bigr)\;\;\forall\,v_{i}\!\in\!\mathcal{S}_{q}\,, (4)

where r¯q\bar{r}_{q} is the mean reward of the nn rollouts of qq and (r¯ℬt,σr,ℬt)(\bar{r}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}},\sigma_{r,\mathcal{B}_{t}}) are statistics over all rollouts of the batch, with (η,ϵ)=(0.1,10−8)(\eta,\epsilon)\!=\!(0.1,10^{-8}). Hyperedges grow whenever a high-reward question retrieves two or more skills jointly, and a periodic pruning step removes every node whose EMA advantage falls below a threshold uminu_{\min}; together, the node and hyperedge updates of round tt read:

𝒱t+1={vi∈𝒱t∪𝒱tnew:ui≥umin},ℰt+1=ℰt∪ℰtrec∪{𝒮q:r¯q≥ρ,|𝒮q|≥2},\mathcal{V}_{t+1}\;=\;\bigl\{\,v_{i}\!\in\!\mathcal{V}_{t}\!\cup\!\mathcal{V}_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}\,:\,u_{i}\!\geq\!u_{\min}\,\bigr\}\,,\qquad\mathcal{E}_{t+1}\;=\;\mathcal{E}_{t}\,\cup\,\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\mathrm{rec}}\,\cup\,\bigl\{\,\mathcal{S}_{q}\,:\,\bar{r}_{q}\!\geq\!\rho,\;|\mathcal{S}_{q}|\!\geq\!2\,\bigr\}\,, (5)

with umin=−0.5u_{\min}\!=\!-0.5 and ℰtrec\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\mathrm{rec}} the round-tt recipes. Each hyperedge records its own EMA advantage w⁡(ej)w(e_{j}), updated by Eq. (4) when its members are again retrieved together for a high-reward question.

Advantage-Weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion. A query is embedded by ff and matched against the node and hyperedge banks; a reciprocal-rank-fusion scorer [8] boosts each node by its advantage, so high-quality skills overtake more similar but low-utility ones in the ranking [20, 13, 15]:

score⁡(vi,q)=1+12​(ui+1)krrf+rankf​(vi,q),𝒮qpool=Top​-​kcos​(𝒱)∪expandq​(ℰ),\mathrm{score}(v_{i};q)\;=\;\frac{1\,+\,\tfrac{1}{2}(u_{i}\!+\!1)}{k_{\mathrm{rrf}}\,+\,\mathrm{rank}_{f}(v_{i};q)}\,,\qquad\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\mathrm{pool}}\;=\;\mathrm{Top}\text{-}k_{\cos}(\mathcal{V})\,\cup\,\mathrm{expand}_{q}(\mathcal{E})\,, (6)

where rankf​(vi,q)\mathrm{rank}_{f}(v_{i};q) is the rank of viv_{i} under cosine similarity ⟨f⁡(q),f⁡(vi)⟩\langle f(q),f(v_{i})\rangle, krrf=60k_{\mathrm{rrf}}\!=\!60, k=100k\!=\!100 nearest nodes form the candidate pool, and expandq​(ℰ)\mathrm{expand}_{q}(\mathcal{E}) adds the members of hyperedges matching qq, so that in libraries larger than the pool, skills composed with a relevant skill still enter it. Flat dictionaries [2, 3, 50] and frontier filters [1] lack this per-item quality prior and joint composition.

Proposition 2. Advantage-weighted ranking places high-utility skills above merely similar ones.

Proof.

We provide experimental results in §4.3 and §4.5 and proofs in Appendix B.2. ∎

Similarity Floor, Capacity Cap, and Zero-Skill Fallback. Injecting marginal skills from a small, noisy library can be worse than injecting none. A floor τ\tau discards candidates whose cosine to qq is below it, a cap NmaxN_{\max} bounds their number, and an empty result falls back to the skill-free prompt:

𝒮q=Top​-​Nmax​(score⁡(⋅,q),{vi∈𝒮qpool:⟨f⁡(q),f⁡(vi)⟩≥τ}),Nmax=3,\mathcal{S}_{q}\;=\;\mathrm{Top}\text{-}N_{\max}\!\Bigl(\,\mathrm{score}(\,\cdot\,;q)\,,\;\;\bigl\{\,v_{i}\!\in\!\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\mathrm{pool}}\,:\,\langle f(q),f(v_{i})\rangle\!\geq\!\tau\,\bigr\}\,\Bigr)\,,\qquad N_{\max}\!=\!3\,, (7)

where |𝒮q|=0|\mathcal{S}_{q}|\!=\!0 reduces πθ(⋅∣q,m,𝒮q)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!q,m,\mathcal{S}_{q}) to πθ(⋅∣q,m)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!q,m); τ\tau is set per dataset (App. E.7). Retrieved skills enter as a strategy hint (App. A) or a terse list. The protocol skill of C1, when enabled, is added for every question without gating and re-injected after each tool turn with the remaining budget.

Proposition 3. Gating with zero-skill fallback never harms the skill-free pipeline in expectation.

Proof.

We provide experimental results in §4.3 and §4.6 and proofs in Appendix B.3. ∎

3.3 C3: Execution Protocol

Tool Calls and Final Answer. C3 decides how the frozen backbone executes a rollout; it never edits ℋ\mathcal{H}, and its options are set per dataset (App. E.7). A concrete tool prompt names the real tool tag (e.g. <text_search>) instead of a TOOL_TAG placeholder, and a lenient parser also executes copied placeholder forms such as <TOOL_TAG>text_search>q. If a rollout ends without a closed <answer> tag (e.g. once the tool budget is spent), a final-answer turn asks once more. An answer suffix requests the final integer without \boxed{} on math and the option letter on multiple choice.

Evidence and Voting. Question pre-search sends the question verbatim to the text_search tool once, outside the tool budget; locate pages adds the text of the pages the question names and of the top BM25 [38] pages of the question’s own PDF, with no API call; on Omni, time grounding lists the keyframe times and, on multiple choice, an option check asks the model to weigh every option against frames and audio. Self-consistency [43] adds 55 samples at temperature 0.70.7 and keeps their most frequent answer, or the greedy one on a tie or when no sample answers. C3 also sets per-dataset token budgets, and on five datasets its options also apply to the training rollouts that build the library, so the library is learned under the same protocol that serves its test questions (App. E.7).

Closing the Loop. A training iteration on ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} retrieves 𝒮q←ℛ⁡(q,m,ℋt)\mathcal{S}_{q}\!\leftarrow\!\mathcal{R}(q,m,\mathcal{H}_{t}), generates nn rollouts under frozen θ\theta, records their failure types, computes advantages {A^q}\{\hat{A}_{q}\}, admits the probe survivors of Φ∘Ψ\Phi\!\circ\!\Psi, and updates ℋt→ℋt+1\mathcal{H}_{t}\!\to\!\mathcal{H}_{t+1} by EMA, hyperedge growth and pruning, so an auditable delta Δ​ℋ\Delta\mathcal{H} replaces the GRPO gradient step Δ​θ\Delta\theta. At evaluation the library is frozen, and C2 and C3 serve each test question. Defaults are (n,K,η,krrf,Nmax,ρ,umin)=(2,2,0.1,60,3,0.5,−0.5)(n,K,\eta,k_{\mathrm{rrf}},N_{\max},\rho,u_{\min})\!=\!(2,2,0.1,60,3,0.5,-0.5).

4 Experiments

We answer six RQs: RQ1: Does HyperSkill rank first on every dataset? RQ2: What does each component add? RQ3: Does counterfactual distillation keep a compact library of useful skills? RQ4: How does the hypergraph evolve under retrieval feedback? RQ5: How sensitive is gating to τ\tau, NmaxN_{\max} and library size? RQ6: What are HyperSkill’s training cost, library size and latency?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate on HyperSkill-Bench, a collection of 1111 public datasets in four regimes (Appendix D.1): Text reasoning (AIME2024/2025, WebWalkerQA), VL-Web (FVQA, InfoSeek, SimpleVQA, LiveVQA), VL-Doc (DocBench, MMLongBench-Doc) and Omni (OmniVideoBench, WorldSense). The metric is token-level F1F_{1} [37] with answer-shape awareness and a CJK-aware tokeniser that splits Chinese into characters; every cell of Table 2 and Figure 4 is the full-set mean over the dataset’s test questions (3030 for AIME2024/2025, 6464 otherwise; 636636 in total), from one evaluation run per cell, scored by the same rule for every column (Appendix D.2).

Baselines and Ablations. We compare against bare Zero-shot [54] (same tools, no library or C3) and the 66 training-free skill methods of Table 1: TrainingFreeGRPO [2] (experience pool), EvoSkill [1] (frontier set), SkillCraft [3] and AutoSkill [50] (code, tip cards), Memento-Skills [56] and XSkill [17] (memory). Each baseline builds its library on the same 128128 training questions by re-implementing its published procedure (Appendix E), likewise without C3. Three ablations reuse the trained library (Appendix E.5): w/o C1 replaces all distilled content by a generic protocol line, w/o C2 also drops that line, and w/o C3, applied on its own, only resets the C3 execution options to their defaults.

Implementation Details. Every method shares the frozen gemini-2.5-flash-lite [7] backbone with native vision/audio interfaces and the gemini-embedding-2-preview [19] encoder ff, both via OpenRouter. Each HyperSkill library is trained for 11 epoch on 128128 training questions per dataset (deduplicated, seed 4242) with batch size 44, n=2n\!=\!2 rollouts per question, seed 11 and the defaults of §3. Three library-run settings (R1–R3) differ in rollout temperature, early stopping, hint synthesis, probe sampling and training-time floor. Each dataset’s run, floor τ\tau and C3 options are selected on held-out training questions, and each library is then retrained on all 128128 questions (Appendix E.7).

Tool Stack and Decoding. Every method uses the same regime tools: a text_search tool for WebWalkerQA and VL-Web, served by gemini-3.8-flash; images passed to the backbone; a BM25 index over the question’s own PDF for VL-Doc; and uniformly sampled keyframes for Omni, 88 on OmniVideoBench and 3232 plus the audio track on WorldSense. Each question gets at most 33 (Text), 55 (VL) or 88 (Omni) rounds and 22 tool calls. Decoding is greedy at temperature 00 with seed 11. The baselines use 10241024 new tokens (20482048 on AIME2025, 40964096 on WorldSense) and retrieve without a similarity floor; HyperSkill’s token budgets and votes belong to C3. Variance: Appendix D.2.

4.2 Main Results (RQ1)

Overall. HyperSkill is best or tied on all 1111 datasets (Table 2) and lifts the average from 29.029.0 for the strongest baseline, XSkill, to 42.042.0: a +13.0+13.0 absolute / +44.9%+44.9\% relative gain, and +14.6+14.6 over Zero-shot (27.427.4). The six baselines lie within 23.423.4–29.029.0, −4.0-4.0 to +1.6+1.6 around Zero-shot, and each falls below Zero-shot on at least three datasets. HyperSkill is above Zero-shot on every row.

Per-dataset. The margin over the best other column is largest on AIME2024 (+26.7+26.7 over SkillCraft, AutoSkill and Memento-Skills), AIME2025 (+20.0+20.0 over three columns) and OmniVideoBench (+14.3+14.3 over XSkill), and is +11.4+11.4 on InfoSeek, +10.4+10.4 on FVQA and +9.1+9.1 on MMLongBench-Doc. The other five margins are +1.3+1.3 to +4.1+4.1, and their paired bootstrap 95% intervals include zero (Appendix D.2), so we conservatively count these five as ties. RQ2 then ablates C1, C1+C2, or C3 alone to measure how much each of the three components adds to the 11-dataset average.

Per-regime. By regime, HyperSkill’s mean per-dataset lead over the best other column is +16.4+16.4 on Text, +9.2+9.2 on Omni, +6.7+6.7 on VL-Web and +6.6+6.6 on VL-Doc, so HyperSkill leads by more than 66 F1 points in every regime, with the largest lead on the Text regime.

4.3 Ablation Study (RQ2)

The three ablations (Figure 4) lower the 11-dataset average from 42.042.0 to 39.539.5 (w/o C1), 37.837.8 (w/o C2) and 31.631.6 (w/o C3), and every variant stays well above Zero-shot (27.427.4); since every one of the ablations lowers the average, each of the three components is effective. The components act at different stages: C1 distils verified skills and a protocol skill from training failures, C2 delivers them to each test question behind the gate, and C3 makes the frozen backbone call its tools and commit to an answer. Only the full HyperSkill, which combines all three components, reaches the best 11-dataset average, and every ablated variant still exceeds all six baselines (23.423.4–29.029.0), so HyperSkill’s lead over the baselines does not depend on any single one of its components.

4.4 Counterfactual Distillation Effectiveness (RQ3)

Figure 5 examines the counterfactual step-level distillation of §3.1, asking whether it keeps a compact library, whether the probe admits useful skills, and whether the distilled skills help at test time.

Distilled skills are few and useful. Pooled over the 11 libraries, HyperSkill admits 154154 skills, 38%38\% of the 407407 skills of the libraries trained without the probe (panel a), so the probe keeps the library compact. They also help: against w/o C1 (panel c), which swaps in a generic protocol line, HyperSkill gains on 66 of the 88 datasets where the two configurations differ (mean +3.4+3.4 F1), led by OmniVideoBench, LiveVQA and InfoSeek; the other three share one configuration.

A single verification vote sharpens skill admission. On 9696 of the 128128 training questions each of AIME2024, FVQA and OmniVideoBench (panel b), we take the 140140 (question, skill) candidates where the no-skill run fails (F1<0.5\,<\!0.5) and a skill is retrieved, and count a candidate as useful when injecting that skill flips the question to a success. Without the probe (K=0K\!=\!0) 2525 of 140140 candidates are useful (0.1790.179). One counterfactual vote raises pooled precision to 0.2730.273 (6/226/22) and, on OmniVideoBench, from 0.1850.185 to 0.4170.417 (5/125/12). Votes at temperature 0.10.1 are nearly deterministic: a single vote already captures the filtering gain and every K≥1K\!\geq\!1 keeps pooled precision above the no-probe rate; hence the libraries use one vote (R2/R3) or two votes on one failure (R1).

4.5 Hypergraph Evolution under Retrieval Feedback (RQ4)

Figure 6 traces the weighted hypergraph of §3.2 over training, asking how retrieval feedback grows the library and its connectivity and how the advantages uiu_{i} of the admitted skills evolve.

Skills accumulate early and stabilise. In an AIME2024 training re-run with per-round logging (3232 rounds of 44 questions; panel a), the library grows from 00 to 22 skills at round 55 and to 44 at round 2323, where it stays through round 3232; the hyperedges grow from 00 to 11 and reach 44 at round 2727, when the library, taken as a skill–hyperedge graph, reaches 88 nodes and 1010 links. The final 44 skills match the size of the AIME2024 library used in Table 2. Admitted skills start at ui=0.3u_{i}\!=\!0.3 and the EMA of Eq. (4) pulls them toward the batch-normalised advantage, so the mean uiu_{i} moves from 0.300.30 (round 55) to 0.190.19 (round 2323) and 0.0190.019 (round 3232) and stays positive throughout the training re-run.

Advantages keep being refined after admission. In the 11 libraries (panel b), the earlier-admitted half of each library, updated most often, has median ui≈0u_{i}\!\approx\!0 (7373 skills) and the later half +0.143+0.143 (8181 skills): the gap (≈0.15\approx\!0.15) grows with the EMA updates that pull each uiu_{i} from 0.30.3 toward A^q\hat{A}_{q}.

4.6 Sensitivity of Gated Retrieval (RQ5)

Figure 7 varies one setting at a time around the frozen configuration of InfoSeek and OmniVideoBench, which cover the image-based VL-Web and the video-based Omni regimes (6464 test questions per cell, single runs). The floor τ\tau takes six values around its frozen value on each dataset (InfoSeek on the hub-corrected scale of Appendix E.7), Nmax∈{1,3,5}N_{\max}\!\in\!\{1,3,5\}, and the library subsets are nested random subsets with 2525, 5050, 7575 and 100%100\% of the skills, where a hyperedge is kept only if all its member skills are kept; ungated retrieval sets τ=−9\tau\!=\!-9. This is a post-hoc sensitivity analysis on the test split; it does not change the frozen per-dataset configuration or the reported results of Table 2.

The frozen settings lie in a stable region. Around the frozen floor (panel a), InfoSeek stays between 40.2040.20 and 45.8045.80 F1 (44.8244.82 at its hub-corrected τ~=−0.02\tilde{\tau}\!=\!-0.02), and OmniVideoBench gives 31.4731.47 at every τ≤0.55\tau\!\leq\!0.55, where injected skills are identical, and 28.3328.33–29.9529.95 at the two larger values.

The floor controls injection. The zero-skill fraction is 00 at the frozen τ\tau on both datasets and rises to 0.630.63 and 0.550.55 at the largest τ\tau, where on average 0.700.70 and 0.780.78 skills are injected per question.

A small capacity cap suffices. Nmax=3N_{\max}\!=\!3 is best or near-best on both datasets (panel b): 44.8244.82 vs 40.9340.93 at 11 and 43.8743.87 at 55 on InfoSeek, and 31.4731.47 vs 31.5131.51 at 11 and 28.4028.40 at 55 on OmniVideoBench, with 11, 33 and up to 55 skills injected per question at the three cap values, respectively.

Gated, the full library is best. With gating (panel c), the full library gives the highest F1 on both datasets (44.8244.82 on InfoSeek, 31.4731.47 on OmniVideoBench), +4.1+4.1 and +3.1+3.1 over the 75%75\% subset; at full size, gated and ungated retrieval give 44.8244.82 vs 44.6444.64 on InfoSeek and 31.4731.47 vs 31.4731.47 on OmniVideoBench, where the injected skills coincide, so gating lowers F1 on neither dataset.

4.7 Cost Analysis (RQ6)

Figure 8 reports two deployment-relevant costs of HyperSkill on all 1111 datasets: the training-API spend to build each library and the size of the learned library in skills and hyperedges; we also compare the per-question inference latency of HyperSkill with Zero-shot on three datasets.

Cheap to train, compact to store. HyperSkill’s library costs $0.12\$0.12–$0.88\$0.88 per dataset to train (mean $0.51\$0.51, total $5.56\$5.56, of which $2.48\$2.48 is knowledge search) and holds 22–4343 skills (mean 14.014.0) and 00–5858 hyperedges; one test pass over all 11 datasets costs $2.34\$2.34. Panel (a) adds the Zero-shot (27.427.4) and HyperSkill (42.042.0) averages, and panel (b) sorts the datasets by library size, with the mean in the last row; the two Omni libraries are the largest (4343 and 3737 skills), and the 154154 skills pooled over all 1111 libraries are 38%38\% of the 407407 skills of the libraries trained without the probe (§4.4). Training needs no gradient step: each library is built from API calls alone, and per question the counterfactual check of C1 adds at most 2​|𝒱~q|2|\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}| verification calls at K=2K\!=\!2 (Eq. (8)), which take the place of the backward pass of standard GRPO (Appendix A) and are already included in the training costs above.

Inference latency stays close to Zero-shot. Measured for HyperSkill and Zero-shot on 1616 test questions per timed dataset with the same harness, mean latency per question is 14.9814.98 vs 11.7511.75 s on AIME2024, 12.7812.78 vs 14.5614.56 s on FVQA and 3.563.56 vs 3.663.66 s on DocBench: HyperSkill adds at most about 33 s (on AIME2024) and is on par or slightly faster elsewhere, since API, tool and network time dominate and C1 and C3 add only short instruction texts to the prompt (Appendix A). The timed datasets cover three regimes (Text, VL-Web and VL-Doc), each with its own tools (§4.1).

5 Conclusion

HyperSkill is a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that evolves a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library through training-time distillation (C1), gated hypergraph retrieval (C2) and an execution protocol (C3). Without parameter updates, it is best or tied on all 1111 datasets (avg. 42.042.0, +13.0+13.0 over the strongest baseline), and every skill stays readable and editable. Each component raises the average, counterfactual distillation keeps a compact library (154154 vs 407407 skills), and the gate settings lie in a stable region. A library costs at most $0.88\$0.88 to train, a full test pass costs $2.34\$2.34, and latency stays close to Zero-shot. Future work includes pairing the library with lightweight parameter updates, sharing it across related datasets and domains, and extending C3 to new tool types and modalities.
