Appendix

Appendix A Prompts Used in HyperSkill

This appendix lists the LLM prompts invoked by HyperSkill, mirroring the prompt-card presentation of HyperGraphRAG [26]. Prompts are grouped by the role they play in the loop of §3: (a) Frozen-Backbone Inference (§3) consumed by every skill-augmented rollout, (b) C1 Skill Distillation (§3.1) that admits counterfactually checked skill nodes, (c) C2 Gated Retrieval Injection (§3.2) that surfaces a question-aware strategy hint, and (d) the C1 protocol skill and the C3 execution texts (§3.3). The weighted hypergraph evolution inside C2 is deliberately prompt-free: per-node advantage EMA, hyperedge growth and the periodic uminu_{\min} safeguard prune are closed-form operators on the rollout reward and never call πθ\pi_{\theta}, so no prompt card appears for that block. Every prompt below is reproduced from the released code (markdown emphasis, dashes and symbols normalised to plain text), with {x} denoting a runtime placeholder; the user-message wrapper around each system prompt is kept compact since the system prompt already constrains the output schema.

A.1 Frozen-Backbone Inference Prompts

Prompt P1: Base Reasoning (REASONING_PROMPT, used on tool-free Text datasets (AIME)). The answer-only base prompt of tool-free datasets; like P2/P3, it is used without retrieved skills whenever Eq. (7) returns the empty skill set (the zero-skill fallback of §3.2), and with the P8 tip line otherwise.

Answer the following question. Output ONLY your final answer inside
<answer>...</answer> tags. Do NOT show your work.

Prompt P2: Search Agent (SEARCH_AGENT_PROMPT, used on Text/VL tool tasks with the text_search / BM25 channels of §4.1). Drives the per-question multi-round loop in which the agent either commits to an answer or emits exactly one tool tag per round under the regime cap (3 rounds on Text, 5 on VL; Omni datasets use P3) and the shared budget of 22 tool calls.

You are an expert research assistant equipped with search tools.
Analyze the question and decide whether to search for more information
or to provide a final answer directly.
{tool_desc}

You must respond in ONE of the following formats:

  Format A - Direct answer (when confident):
    <reason>...</reason>
    <answer>...</answer>

  Format B - Search for more information:
    <reason>...</reason>
    <TOOL_TAG>specific query</TOOL_TAG>

Replace TOOL_TAG with one of the available tools listed above.

On WebWalkerQA, for every method, the last two lines of P2 read <text_search>specific query</text_search> and “Put the search query itself between the <text_search> and </text_search> tags.”

Prompt P3: Omni Agent (OMNI_AGENT_PROMPT, used on the Omni regime). The omnimodal counterpart of P2: keeps the same two-format response schema while explicitly instructing the backbone to fuse text, image, audio transcript, and video keyframes in one multimodal call.

You are an expert multimodal reasoning assistant. You can process text,
images, audio transcripts, and video descriptions. Analyze all provided
modalities together to derive a precise answer.
{tool_desc}

You must respond in ONE of the following formats:

  Format A - Direct answer (when confident):
    <reason>...</reason>
    <answer>...</answer>

  Format B - Search for more information:
    <reason>...</reason>
    <TOOL_TAG>specific query</TOOL_TAG>

Replace TOOL_TAG with one of the available tools listed above.

Prompt P4: After-Search Continuation (AFTER_SEARCH_PROMPT). Re-enters the agent into another reasoning round with the original question and the freshly retrieved evidence; iterated until the regime-specific round cap (33, 55 or 88) is reached or an <answer> tag closes the reasoning trace.

Based on the search results provided, continue your reasoning and either
search again (if needed) or provide the final answer.

Original question: {question}

{search_results}

Now provide your next step:

A.2 C1: Skill Distillation Prompts (§3.1)

Prompt P5: Contrastive Step Alignment (Φ\Phi in Eq. (2), SKILL_CONTRASTIVE_EXTRACT). Operates on the success/failure split at threshold ρ=0.5\rho\!=\!0.5: aligns numbered reasoning steps across the two buckets, marks divergence points, and harvests both atomic skills and multi-skill recipes that successes exhibit but failures jointly miss; recipes feed downstream hyperedge construction in §3.2.

[system]
You are an expert at analyzing reasoning trajectories to extract reusable
skills. Your task: given a question with GOOD attempts (high reward) and
BAD attempts (low reward), perform step-level contrastive analysis to
find exactly WHERE and WHY the good attempts succeeded.
<Instructions>
1. Decompose each attempt into numbered reasoning steps.
2. Align steps across good and bad attempts - find corresponding steps
   that address the same sub-problem.
3. Identify divergence points - the specific steps where good and bad
   attempts DIFFER in strategy or correctness.
4. Extract atomic skills - from each divergence point, extract the
   generalizable skill that the good attempt used (NOT specific to
   this question).
5. Identify skill recipes - if multiple atomic skills worked TOGETHER
   in successful attempts but were missing together in failures, group
   them as a recipe.
</Instructions>
<Output Format>
<Step Alignment>
[Show the aligned steps of good vs bad attempts, marking divergence
 points with *]
</Step Alignment>
<Divergence Analysis>
[For each divergence point: what the good attempt did vs what the bad
 attempt did, and WHY the good approach worked]
</Divergence Analysis>
<Atomic Skills>
[One per line, extracted from divergence points:]
SKILL: <name (3-7 words)> | <what to do and when (1-2 sentences)>
</Atomic Skills>
<Skill Recipes>
[Combinations of atomic skills that must be used TOGETHER for success:]
RECIPE: <recipe name> | <skill_1 + skill_2 + ...> |
        <when to apply this combination>
</Skill Recipes>
</Output Format>

[user]
<Question>{question}</Question>
<Gold Answer>{gold_answer}</Gold Answer>
<Good Attempts>{good_attempts}</Good Attempts>
<Bad Attempts>{bad_attempts}</Bad Attempts>
Perform step-level contrastive analysis as instructed.

Prompt P6: Counterfactual Verification (SKILL_COUNTERFACTUAL_VERIFY; KK-probe vote of Eq. (3)). Each candidate emitted by P5 is paired with up to K=2K\!=\!2 failure probes of its own question (Appendix E.7) and admitted only when a strict majority of probes return YES; the md5\mathrm{md5} name identifier then deduplicates the increment 𝒱tnew\mathcal{V}_{t}^{\mathrm{new}} against 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}, so a repeated skill name is skipped.

[system]
You are evaluating whether a proposed reasoning skill would help an
agent that FAILED a question.
Given:
- A question the agent got WRONG
- The agent’s FAILED reasoning trajectory
- A proposed SKILL
Judge: If the agent had known and applied this skill, would it likely
have answered correctly?
Output EXACTLY one line:
VERDICT: YES | <confidence 0-1> | <brief reason>
or
VERDICT: NO | <confidence 0-1> | <brief reason>

[user]
<Question>{question}</Question>
<Gold Answer>{gold_answer}</Gold Answer>
<Failed Trajectory>{failed_trajectory}</Failed Trajectory>
<Proposed Skill>{skill}</Proposed Skill>
Would this skill have helped? Output VERDICT line only.

A.3 C2: Gated Retrieval Injection Prompts (§3.2)

Prompt P7: Strategy Hint Synthesis (SKILL_SUMMARY_PROMPT). After the advantage-weighted RRF of Eq. (6) and the similarity/capacity gates of Eq. (7) yield a non-empty 𝒮q\mathcal{S}_{q}, this prompt distils the retrieved skills into a question-aware 22–33 sentence hint that emphasises how to combine them rather than enumerating them, so that the context injected into the prompt stays short.

Given a question and a set of retrieved reasoning skills, write a concise
strategy hint (2-3 sentences) that synthesizes these skills specifically
for this question. Focus on HOW to combine them, not just listing them.
Question: {question}
Retrieved Skills:
{skills_raw}
Strategy hint (2-3 sentences, actionable):

With the schema-constrained hint (SimpleVQA), the following constraint is inserted before the last line of P7; the bracketed clause is added only in tool regimes, with {limit} the tool budget.

Constraints for the hint: it must not change the required output format
(the agent ends with a short final answer inside <answer>...</answer>, as
short as the question allows, never a full sentence when a name, number
or phrase suffices). [It must not ask for more than {limit} tool calls in
total, and the agent must always finish with a final <answer> even if a
search did not find everything.]

Prompt P8: Skill-Augmented Wrapper (SKILL_AUGMENTED_PROMPT). The hint produced by P7 is prepended to the inference prompt of P1/P2/P3 as a single tip line; whenever |𝒮q|=0|\mathcal{S}_{q}|\!=\!0 no retrieved skill enters this wrapper, which then carries only the protocol skill or is skipped; this is the zero-skill fallback that Proposition 3 analyses, with no P7 call for such zero-skill questions.

Tip from prior experience: {skills_context}

A.4 C1 Protocol-Skill and C3 Execution Texts (§3.1, §3.3)

These texts are reproduced verbatim from the released code (strategies/protocol.py, prompting.py, presearch.py, locate_pages.py, video.py); {x} is a runtime placeholder and [...] names the condition under which a line is used; all remaining text is fixed.

Prompt P9: Protocol Skill (C1, injected with the skills context). Instruction lines for the failure types kept in training (at least 22 occurrences; no_answer adds none of its own), followed by one answer-form line with word limit {words} =max⁡(200,⌊0.45⋅max new tokens⌋)=\max(200,\lfloor 0.45\cdot\text{max new tokens}\rfloor).

Output protocol (learned from training failures): <lines below>
[malformed_tool] To call a tool, put the query inside that tool’s own
  tag, exactly like <{tag}>your query</{tag}>; the tag name is the tool
  name (never write TOOL_TAG and never nest tags).
[over_budget or malformed_tool] Use at most {budget} tool calls in
  total; after the last one, or as soon as you can answer, stop calling
  tools and give your best final answer.
[tool_without_tools] No tool is available for this question: do not
  write any tool call, search request or TOOL_TAG; answer directly from
  the given input.
[math] Reason concisely (the whole response must stay well under
  {words} words) and end with the final integer inside
  <answer>...</answer>; do not use \boxed{}.
[short / default] Always end with your final answer inside
  <answer>...</answer>, as short as the question allows (a name, number,
  short phrase or option letter, not a full sentence).
[data form, option letters] Always end with only the option letter of
  your choice inside <answer>...</answer> (e.g. <answer>B</answer>).
[data form, long golds] Always end with your final answer inside
  <answer>...</answer>, written as one complete sentence (about {n}
  words) that restates the key terms of the question together with the
  answer.
[data form, frequent abstention] If the input does not contain the
  answer, answer exactly <answer>{frequent}</answer>.

Prompt P10: Protocol Re-injection (C1/C2, after each tool turn, inside the “--- Updated Skills ---” block). Appended to every tool result while the protocol skill is on (line 7 of Algorithm 4), so that both the remaining tool budget and the required final-answer tag stay in view.

[calls left] Protocol: you may make {left} more tool call(s), written as
  <{tag}>your query</{tag}>; if the results above suffice, give the
  final answer inside <answer>...</answer> now.
[budget spent] Protocol: you have used all {budget} tool calls. Do not
  call a tool again; give your best final answer now inside
  <answer>...</answer>.

Prompt P11: Final-Answer Turn (C3). {form} is “ (only the final integer)” on math, “ (only the option letter)” on multiple choice, and empty otherwise; the turn is sent at most once per rollout.

[budget spent or repeated query] Tool budget exhausted: no further tool
  call will be executed. Based on the information above, give your final
  answer now inside <answer>...</answer>{form}.
[otherwise] You have not given your final answer yet. Give it now inside
  <answer>...</answer>{form}.

Prompt P12: Answer Suffix and Concrete Tool Prompt (C3). The suffix follows the question. The concrete tool prompt replaces the TOOL_TAG lines of P2/P3 by the real tag and one example; without tools (Omni), it drops the search format instead; the lenient parser accepts placeholders.

[math] Reason step by step, then end your response with the final
  integer inside <answer>...</answer> (for example <answer>N</answer>
  for the integer N); do not use \boxed{}.
[multiple choice] End your response with only the letter of the correct
  option inside <answer>...</answer> (for example <answer>X</answer> for
  option X).
[concrete tool prompt, Format B] <{tag}>specific query</{tag}>
  The tag is the tool’s own name. Example of a correct tool call:
  <text_search>Eiffel Tower height in metres</text_search>

Prompt P13: Evidence Texts (C3: question pre-search, locate pages, time grounding, option check). Each text is added only when the dataset enables the matching C3 option (QP, PGnn, TG, OC in Appendix E.7); the pre-search call is not counted against the per-question tool budget.

[pre-search] Results of a knowledge search for the question itself (run
  automatically before your first step):
  [text_search Results]
  {results}
  Use these results if they answer the question; otherwise search
  further.
[locate pages] Candidate pages of {pdf}, located by document search for
  this question (text extracted from the PDF): [page k] {text} ...
  Answer from these pages. If they do not contain the answer, search the
  document again with <doc_search>...</doc_search>. Answer "Not
  answerable" only if the information is still not found after
  searching. Put the final answer inside <answer>...</answer>.
[time grounding] Video timing: the video lasts {T}. The {n} images are
  keyframes in temporal order, taken at image 1 = {t1}, ... The audio
  track covers the whole video on the same timeline (0:00 to {T}). For
  questions about when something happens, compare its time with the
  total length: the beginning is the first third, the middle the second
  third and the end the last third. Between two keyframes, rely on the
  audio and the neighbouring frames.
[option check] Before answering, check every option against what the
  frames show and what the audio says: for each option write one short
  line ’X: supported / contradicted / no evidence’ with the frame time
  or the audio it relies on, then choose the best-supported option.
  Choose an option such as ’not sure’, ’unknown’, ’it is unclear’ or
  ’none of the above’ only if every other option is contradicted. Never
  decline to answer: always end with exactly one option letter inside
  <answer>...</answer>, for example <answer>B</answer>.

A.5 Per-Baseline Injection Formats and Per-Question Call Budget

Injection formats. Each training-free baseline of §4.1 builds its own library (Appendix E) and injects its retrieved entries in its own surface form, prepended to the shared inference prompt. The forms, reproduced from the released baseline code with their retrieval depth in parentheses, are:

trainingfreegrpo : When solving problems, you MUST first carefully read
                   and understand the helpful instructions and
                   experiences: [<id>]. <experience> ...        (top-10)
skillcraft       : Reusable skills (procedures composed from your
                   operations; apply the most relevant one, then answer
                   in the required format): ‘‘‘python <code>‘‘‘  (top-3)
autoskill        : Relevant skill cards from prior experience:
                   * Skill: <name> -- <description>
                     * Tip: <tip> ...                             (top-3)
evoskill         : > [frontier-skill, val_gain=<gain>] <name>: <desc>
                      1. <instruction> ...                        (top-3)
mementoskills    : [Memory 1] Recall a similar past case:
                   <markdown skill file>                          (top-1)
xskill           : <> Cross-task experiences: - <experience> ...  (top-3)
                   <> Skill (<name>): 1. <step> ...               (top-1)

Per-question LLM call budget. For one round-tt batch question qq with n=2n\!=\!2 skill-augmented rollouts under regime cap R∈{3,5,8}R\!\in\!\{3,5,8\}, the prompts P1–P13 above together fire at most

𝟏[|𝒮q|>0]+n(R+1)⏟inference+1⏟distillation+K​|𝒱~q|⏟verification\underbrace{\mathbf{1}\bigl[|\mathcal{S}_{q}|>0\bigr]+n\,(R{+}1)}_{\text{inference}}\;+\;\underbrace{1}_{\text{distillation}}\;+\;\underbrace{K\,|\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}|}_{\text{verification}} (8)

LLM calls: P7 once for hint synthesis when the gates of Eq. (7) admit at least one skill, then P1/P2/P3 followed by up to R−1R{-}1 P4 continuations and at most one final-answer turn per rollout; P5 on the nn-rollout pool whenever at least one success and one failure coexist; and P6 once per (candidate, failure-probe) pair, i.e. at most 2​|𝒱~q|2|\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}| calls at K=2K\!=\!2. P8 is a one-line wrapper that fires zero LLM calls. Compared to the backward pass of standard GRPO, this replaces Δ​θ\Delta\theta with 𝒪⁡(|𝒱~q|)\mathcal{O}(|\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}|) frozen-backbone calls per question, which benefit from prompt caching since the P5/P6 system messages are identical across calls and only the question, trajectories and candidate skill change per call.

Reproducibility. The prompts above, with Eqs. (2)–(3) and the closed-form operators of Eqs. (4)–(7), specify HyperSkill’s LLM surface on the unified gemini-2.5-flash-lite backbone (§4.1). Evaluation decodes at temperature 00 (self-consistency samples at 0.70.7); training rollouts use temperature 0.40.4 in library runs R2/R3 and 0.70.7 (Text) / 1.01.0 (VL, Omni) in run R1, distillation 0.30.3, verification 0.10.1, and hint synthesis 00. The default hyperparameters are (n,K,η,krrf,Nmax,ρ,umin)=(2,2,0.1,60,3,0.5,−0.5)(n,K,\eta,k_{\mathrm{rrf}},N_{\max},\rho,u_{\min})\!=\!(2,2,0.1,60,3,0.5,-0.5) with protocol threshold 22; the per-dataset floor τ\tau, injection variants and C3 options are listed in Appendix E.7, together with the library run of each dataset.

Appendix B Proofs of Propositions

This appendix proves Propositions 1–3 stated in §3, formalising the three claims that ground counterfactual step-level skill distillation (C1, §3.1), the advantage-weighted hypergraph retrieval of C2 (§3.2), and its gate with zero-skill fallback (C2, §3.2). Notation follows §3: πθ\pi_{\theta} is the frozen omnimodal backbone, ℋ=(𝒱,ℰ,w)\mathcal{H}\!=\!(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},w) the weighted skill hypergraph with per-node advantage ui∈[−1,1]u_{i}\!\in\![-1,1], ℛ\mathcal{R} the retriever, ff the shared encoder, and r∈[0,1]r\!\in\![0,1] the token-level F1F_{1} reward against a∗a^{*}.

B.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proposition 1. Counterfactual distillation favours failure-rescuing skills over co-occurring ones.

Proof.

Fix a question q∈ℬtq\!\in\!\mathcal{B}_{t} and let 𝒱~q\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q} be the candidate set returned by the contrastive aligner of Eq. (2). Each candidate v~\widetilde{v} has an unobserved counterfactual success probability

pv~=Pr[πθ(⋅∣v~,q,a∗,o−)=YES|o−∼Unif(𝒪q−)]∈[0,1],p_{\widetilde{v}}\;=\;\Pr\!\bigl[\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!\widetilde{v},q,a^{*},o^{-})\!=\!\mathrm{YES}\,\big|\,o^{-}\!\sim\!\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{O}_{q}^{-})\bigr]\;\in\;[0,1], (9)

which separates candidates into a failure-rescuing cohort 𝒦={v~:pv~>12}\mathcal{K}\!=\!\{\widetilde{v}:p_{\widetilde{v}}\!>\!\tfrac{1}{2}\} and a correlation cohort 𝒩=𝒱~q∖𝒦\mathcal{N}\!=\!\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}\!\setminus\!\mathcal{K} with pv~≤12p_{\widetilde{v}}\!\leq\!\tfrac{1}{2}; the YES verdict is the operational criterion for rescue, which RQ3(b) checks against observed flips. Modelling the KK probes of Eq. (3) as i.i.d. draws o1−,…,oK−∈𝒪q−o_{1}^{-},\dots,o_{K}^{-}\!\in\!\mathcal{O}_{q}^{-} and writing SK(v~)=∑ℓ𝟏[πθ(⋅∣v~,q,a∗,oℓ−)=YES]∼Binomial(K,pv~)S_{K}(\widetilde{v})\!=\!\sum_{\ell}\mathbf{1}[\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!\widetilde{v},q,a^{*},o_{\ell}^{-})\!=\!\mathrm{YES}]\!\sim\!\mathrm{Binomial}(K,p_{\widetilde{v}}), the admission rule of Eq. (3) selects the survivors of a strict majority vote over the KK probes of each candidate:

𝒱tnew={v~∈𝒱~q:SK​(v~)>K/2},α⁡(p)=∑j=⌊K/2⌋+1K(Kj)​pj​(−p)K−j,\mathcal{V}_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}\!=\!\bigl\{\widetilde{v}\!\in\!\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}\!:\,S_{K}(\widetilde{v})\!>\!K/2\bigr\},\;\;\alpha(p)\!=\!\!\!\!\sum_{j=\lfloor K/2\rfloor+1}^{K}\!\!\binom{K}{j}p^{j}(1\!-\!p)^{K-j}, (10)

so the admission rate of any candidate is

Pr[v~∈𝒱tnew]=α(pv~).\Pr\bigl[\widetilde{v}\in\mathcal{V}_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}\bigr]\;=\;\alpha(p_{\widetilde{v}}). (11)

Because α\alpha is strictly increasing, the gap between cohorts is strict for every K≥1K\!\geq\!1, and for odd KK (including the single probe of runs R2/R3) α\alpha crosses 12\tfrac{1}{2} exactly at p=12p\!=\!\tfrac{1}{2}, so the two cohorts separate:

minv~∈𝒦α(pv~)>maxv~∈𝒩α(pv~),α(pv~)→𝟏[pv~>12]asK→∞(pv~≠12),\min_{\widetilde{v}\in\mathcal{K}}\alpha(p_{\widetilde{v}})\;>\;\max_{\widetilde{v}\in\mathcal{N}}\alpha(p_{\widetilde{v}}),\qquad\alpha(p_{\widetilde{v}})\!\to\!\mathbf{1}[p_{\widetilde{v}}\!>\!\tfrac{1}{2}]\;\text{as}\;K\!\to\!\infty\;\;(p_{\widetilde{v}}\!\neq\!\tfrac{1}{2}), (12)

where the limit follows from Hoeffding’s inequality on |SK/K−pv~||S_{K}/K-p_{\widetilde{v}}|. Letting β=Prv~[v~∈𝒦]∈(0,1)\beta\!=\!\Pr_{\widetilde{v}}[\widetilde{v}\!\in\!\mathcal{K}]\!\in\!(0,1) denote the prior failure-rescuing fraction of 𝒱~q\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}, the library precision after admission obeys

Prec⁡(K)=β​𝔼v~∈𝒦​[α⁡(pv~)]β​𝔼v~∈𝒦​[α⁡(pv~)]+(−β)​𝔼v~∈𝒩​[α⁡(pv~)]>β=Prec⁡(0),\mathrm{Prec}(K)\;=\;\frac{\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{v}\in\mathcal{K}}[\alpha(p_{\widetilde{v}})]}{\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{v}\in\mathcal{K}}[\alpha(p_{\widetilde{v}})]\,+\,(1\!-\!\beta)\,\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{v}\in\mathcal{N}}[\alpha(p_{\widetilde{v}})]}\;>\;\beta\;=\;\mathrm{Prec}(0), (13)

since 𝔼𝒦​[α]>𝔼𝒩​[α]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{K}}[\alpha]\!>\!\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}}[\alpha] by Eq. (12), where Prec⁡(0)\mathrm{Prec}(0) is the precision without the probe. Eq. (13) further yields Prec⁡(K)→1\mathrm{Prec}(K)\!\to\!1 as K→∞K\!\to\!\infty if no candidate has pv~=12p_{\widetilde{v}}\!=\!\tfrac{1}{2}, so the counterfactual gate raises admission precision, in this model, above the base rate of the candidate pool. Empirically (§4.4), a single vote raises pooled precision from 0.1790.179 to 0.2730.273; larger KK still keeps the precision above the no-probe base rate (0.2140.214 at K=3,5K\!=\!3,5 vs 0.1790.179, pooled over three datasets), as Proposition 1 requires. ∎

B.2 Proof of Proposition 2

Proposition 2. Advantage-weighted ranking places high-utility skills above merely similar ones.

Proof.

Fix a query qq and two skills va,vb∈𝒱v_{a},v_{b}\!\in\!\mathcal{V} with cosine similarities sa=⟨f⁡(q),f⁡(va)⟩s_{a}\!=\!\langle f(q),f(v_{a})\rangle and sb=⟨f⁡(q),f⁡(vb)⟩s_{b}\!=\!\langle f(q),f(v_{b})\rangle, and write κi=rankf​(vi,q)\kappa_{i}\!=\!\mathrm{rank}_{f}(v_{i};q) for the rank under plain similarity. Under plain similarity, retrieval order depends only on the rank pair (κa,κb)(\kappa_{a},\kappa_{b}) of the two skills:

scoreplain​(vi,q)=−κi,scoreplain​(va,q)−scoreplain​(vb,q)=κb−κa,\mathrm{score}_{\mathrm{plain}}(v_{i};q)\;=\;-\kappa_{i},\qquad\mathrm{score}_{\mathrm{plain}}(v_{a};q)\!-\!\mathrm{score}_{\mathrm{plain}}(v_{b};q)\;=\;\kappa_{b}\!-\!\kappa_{a}, (14)

so any utility difference is ignored. Under the advantage-weighted RRF rule of Eq. (6),

score⁡(vi,q)=1+12​(ui+1)krrf+κi,ui∈[−1,1],κi≥1,krrf=60,\mathrm{score}(v_{i};q)\;=\;\frac{1\,+\,\tfrac{1}{2}(u_{i}\!+\!1)}{k_{\mathrm{rrf}}\,+\,\kappa_{i}}\,,\qquad u_{i}\!\in\![-1,1],\;\;\kappa_{i}\!\geq\!1,\;\;k_{\mathrm{rrf}}\!=\!60, (15)

the per-skill score factorises into a similarity-rank kernel 1/(krrf+κi)1/(k_{\mathrm{rrf}}\!+\!\kappa_{i}) and an advantage prior +ui+12=3+ui2∈[1,2]1\!+\!\tfrac{u_{i}+1}{2}\!=\!\tfrac{3+u_{i}}{2}\!\in\![1,2], so a less similar skill vbv_{b} (κb>κa\kappa_{b}\!>\!\kappa_{a}) is ranked above vav_{a} exactly when its advantage prior outweighs the rank gap between the two similarity kernels,

score(vb;q)>score(va;q)⟺3+ub3+ua>krrf+κbkrrf+κa,\mathrm{score}(v_{b};q)\;>\;\mathrm{score}(v_{a};q)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{3+u_{b}}{3+u_{a}}\;>\;\frac{k_{\mathrm{rrf}}+\kappa_{b}}{k_{\mathrm{rrf}}+\kappa_{a}}, (16)

which is the per-item quality signal that flat similarity cannot expose; with krrf=60k_{\mathrm{rrf}}\!=\!60, a skill one rank lower overtakes its neighbour once its prior is larger by a factor above +1/(+κa)1\!+\!1/(60\!+\!\kappa_{a}). To see that uiu_{i} tracks utility, observe that the EMA update of Eq. (4) admits a contraction-mapping fixed-point analysis: let r¯i,t\bar{r}_{i,t} be the mean reward of the question that retrieved viv_{i} at round tt; with the advantage and recursion of Eq. (4),

A^i,t=tanh⁡(r¯i,t−r¯ℬtσr,ℬt+ϵ)∈(−1,1),ui,t+1=(−η)​ui,t+η​A^i,t,\hat{A}_{i,t}\;=\;\tanh\Bigl(\frac{\bar{r}_{i,t}-\bar{r}_{\mathcal{B}_{t}}}{\sigma_{r,\mathcal{B}_{t}}+\epsilon}\Bigr)\in(-1,1),\qquad u_{i,t+1}\;=\;(1\!-\!\eta)\,u_{i,t}+\eta\,\hat{A}_{i,t}, (17)

the EMA recursion yields, by stationarity of the rollout distribution,

limt→∞𝔼⁡[ui,t]=𝔼⁡[A^i,∞],𝔼⁡[A^i,∞]> 0​if​Δi​is symmetric about a positive mean,\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[u_{i,t}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\hat{A}_{i,\infty}\bigr],\qquad\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat{A}_{i,\infty}\bigr]\;>\;0\;\;\text{if}\;\;\Delta_{i}\;\text{is symmetric about a positive mean}, (18)

where Δi\Delta_{i} is the argument of tanh\tanh in Eq. (17) and the implication holds because tanh\tanh is odd and increasing; so 𝔼⁡[ui,∞]>0\mathbb{E}[u_{i,\infty}]\!>\!0 when retrieving viv_{i} goes with above-average rewards. Combining Eq. (16) with Eq. (18), skills of nearby rank are ordered by their long-run utility, and the multiplicative prior of Eq. (15) cannot be replicated by any rank-only retriever, including the median-frontier filter ℒfrt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{frt}} of EvoSkill, which exposes only a binary quality cut. Hence Proposition 2 is established. ∎

B.3 Proof of Proposition 3

Proposition 3. Gating with zero-skill fallback never harms the skill-free pipeline in expectation.

Proof.

Let ZS(q)=πθ(⋅∣q,m)\mathrm{ZS}(q)\!=\!\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!q,m) denote the skill-free pipeline (no retrieved skill; protocol skill and C3 options unchanged) and HS(q,𝒮q)=πθ(⋅∣q,m,𝒮q)\mathrm{HS}(q,\mathcal{S}_{q})\!=\!\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!q,m,\mathcal{S}_{q}) the gated skill-augmented policy of Eq. (7), with reward r⁡(π,q,a∗)∈[0,1]r(\pi;q,a^{*})\!\in\![0,1]. Partition the query distribution by the gate output,

𝒬0={q:|𝒮q|=0},𝒬1={q:|𝒮q|≥1},p0=Pr⁡[𝒬0],p1=−p0,\mathcal{Q}_{0}\;=\;\bigl\{q\!:\!|\mathcal{S}_{q}|\!=\!0\bigr\},\qquad\mathcal{Q}_{1}\;=\;\bigl\{q\!:\!|\mathcal{S}_{q}|\!\geq\!1\bigr\},\qquad p_{0}\!=\!\Pr[\mathcal{Q}_{0}],\;\;p_{1}\!=\!1\!-\!p_{0}, (19)

where p0p_{0} is exactly the zero-skill fallback rate, reported as the zero-skill fraction in Figure 7(a) (00 at the frozen τ\tau on both datasets, rising to 0.630.63 and 0.550.55 at the largest τ\tau). The fallback clause of Eq. (7) gives a pointwise identity on 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0},

∀q∈𝒬0:HS⁡(q,𝒮q)≡ZS⁡(q)⟹𝔼q∼𝒬0​[r⁡(HS)−r⁡(ZS)]= 0,\forall q\!\in\!\mathcal{Q}_{0}\!:\;\;\mathrm{HS}(q,\mathcal{S}_{q})\;\equiv\;\mathrm{ZS}(q)\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{0}}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{HS})\!-\!r(\mathrm{ZS})\bigr]\;=\;0, (20)

so the zero-skill branch contributes zero difference. On 𝒬1\mathcal{Q}_{1} every injected skill obeys the two gates of Eq. (7),

⟨f⁡(q),f⁡(vi)⟩≥τ∀vi∈𝒮q,|𝒮q|≤Nmax,\langle f(q),f(v_{i})\rangle\;\geq\;\tau\quad\forall v_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{q},\qquad|\mathcal{S}_{q}|\;\leq\;N_{\max}, (21)

so the prompt receives at most NmaxN_{\max} skills each carrying mutual information at least

I(vi;a∗∣q)≥ιτ:=infv:⟨f⁡(q),f⁡(v)⟩≥τI(v;a∗∣q)≥ 0,I\!\bigl(v_{i};a^{*}\!\mid\!q\bigr)\;\geq\;\iota_{\tau}\;:=\;\inf_{v:\langle f(q),f(v)\rangle\geq\tau}\!I(v;a^{*}\!\mid\!q)\;\geq\;0, (22)

where a∗a^{*} is the gold answer and ιτ\iota_{\tau} is the similarity-floor information bound. Under the gate-admissibility assumption that, at budget NmaxN_{\max}, skills clearing both gates do not lower the expected reward of the frozen πθ\pi_{\theta} (formally, 𝔼⁡[r⁡(HS)]≥𝔼⁡[r⁡(ZS)]\mathbb{E}[r(\mathrm{HS})]\!\geq\!\mathbb{E}[r(\mathrm{ZS})] whenever every injected skill clears the floor τ\tau; marginal skills below τ\tau need not, §3.2), the gated branch never lowers the expected reward,

𝔼q∼𝒬1​[r⁡(HS)]≥𝔼q∼𝒬1​[r⁡(ZS)],equality​if​πθ​ignores​the​injections.\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{1}}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{HS})\bigr]\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{1}}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{ZS})\bigr],\quad\mathrm{equality\ if}\;\pi_{\theta}\;\mathrm{ignores\ the\ injections}. (23)

Combining Eq. (20) and Eq. (23) via the law of total expectation yields the unconditional safety bound

𝔼q​[r⁡(HS)]−𝔼q​[r⁡(ZS)]=p1⋅(𝔼q∼𝒬1​[r⁡(HS)−r⁡(ZS)])+p0⋅0≥ 0,\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{HS})\bigr]\;-\;\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{ZS})\bigr]\;=\;p_{1}\!\cdot\!\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{1}}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{HS})\!-\!r(\mathrm{ZS})\bigr]\bigr)\;+\;p_{0}\!\cdot\!0\;\geq\;0, (24)

so HS is no worse than the skill-free pipeline in expectation. The argument is independent of |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|, so it applies uniformly across cold-start (high p0p_{0}, small |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|) and mature regimes (low p0p_{0}, large |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|); on a mature library the bound of Eq. (23) covers most queries, while on a cold-start library Eq. (20) dominates and HS recovers ZS exactly. The same decomposition further yields a quantitative envelope on the gain

0≤𝔼q​[r⁡(HS)−r⁡(ZS)]=p1⋅(𝔼q∼𝒬1​[r⁡(HS)]−𝔼q∼𝒬1​[r⁡(ZS)]),0\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{HS})\!-\!r(\mathrm{ZS})\bigr]\;=\;p_{1}\!\cdot\!\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{1}}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{HS})\bigr]\!-\!\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{1}}\!\bigl[r(\mathrm{ZS})\bigr]\Bigr), (25)

so the improvement scales with the non-fallback mass p1=−p0p_{1}\!=\!1\!-\!p_{0}, and the room for improvement grows as p0p_{0} shrinks. Hence Proposition 3 is established for every library size |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|. ∎

Appendix C HyperSkill Algorithm Details

This appendix expands §3 into executable pseudocode in the algorithm-card style of HyperGraphRAG [26]. Algorithm 1 realises C1 (§3.1, Eqs. (2)–(3)) and records the failure types of the protocol skill; Algorithms 2 and 3 realise the training side (Eqs. (4)–(5)) and the retrieval side (Eqs. (6)–(7)) of C2 (§3.2); and Algorithm 4 realises the execution protocol of C3 (§3.3).

C1: Training-Time Skill Distillation. Each question q∈ℬtq\!\in\!\mathcal{B}_{t} receives nn skill-augmented rollouts, split at ρ\rho into 𝒪q+\mathcal{O}_{q}^{+} and 𝒪q−\mathcal{O}_{q}^{-}. The regex decomposer Ψ\Psi slices each rollout into steps at zero LLM cost, and the aligner Φ\Phi returns the candidate set 𝒱~q\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q} of divergent atomic skills. Each candidate is probed against a list 𝒫q\mathcal{P}_{q} of at most KK failure probes of its own question and is admitted only on a strict majority of YES verdicts; sid\mathrm{sid} deduplicates it against 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t}, and every recipe with at least two admitted members joins ℰtrec\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\mathrm{rec}}. Every rollout that ends without an answer also increments the count cϕc_{\phi} of its failure type ϕ\phi; a type enters the protocol skill (Prompt P9) once cϕ≥2c_{\phi}\!\geq\!2, already for the remaining training rollouts when the skill is on, and the final counts define the protocol skill used at test time.

Complexity Analysis. Per batch, the rollouts cost 𝒪⁡(|ℬt|⋅n)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{B}_{t}|\!\cdot\!n) backbone calls, Ψ\Psi is free, Φ\Phi fires once per group (𝒪⁡(|ℬt|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{B}_{t}|) calls) and the probe adds KK calls per candidate (𝒪⁡(|ℬt|⋅|𝒱~q|⋅K)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{B}_{t}|\!\cdot\!|\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}|\!\cdot\!K)); with (n,K)=(2,2)(n,K)\!=\!(2,2) and an empirical |𝒱~q|≤3|\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{q}|\!\leq\!3, this is at most 66 probes per question, so rollout generation dominates.

C2 (training side): Weighted Hypergraph Evolution. Every admitted skill is embedded by ff and stored in the dual KV/VDB index with initial advantage ui=0.3u_{i}\!=\!0.3. The batch-normalised advantage A^q\hat{A}_{q} of each question drives the EMA of Eq. (4) on its retrieved skills; a high-reward question (r¯q≥ρ\bar{r}_{q}\!\geq\!\rho) that retrieves two or more skills adds them as a hyperedge (or EMA-updates its weight), and a periodic safeguard prune evicts every node with ui<uminu_{i}\!<\!u_{\min}. None of these steps calls the LLM. Training retrieval differs from test retrieval in three ways: it uses an advantage floor of 00, so a skill whose advantage turns negative is no longer reinforced; for VL items its query embedding averages the question and image embeddings; and after each tool call the rollout refreshes its skills (query: question and tool query) in an “Updated Skills” block that receives no EMA credit.

Complexity Analysis. Each batch issues at most |𝒱tnew||\mathcal{V}_{t}^{\mathrm{new}}| skill embedding calls and one per new hyperedge, 𝒪⁡(∑q∈ℬt|𝒮q|)\mathcal{O}(\sum_{q\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}|\mathcal{S}_{q}|) scalar EMA updates, and an 𝒪⁡(|𝒱t+1|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}_{t+1}|) periodic prune; no step calls πθ\pi_{\theta}.

C2 (test side): Gated Retrieval and Injection. Every query qq is embedded by the same encoder ff as the skills. Its k=100k\!=\!100 nearest nodes form the candidate pool, and hyperedges that match qq add their member skills to this pool (scored at 0.8×0.8\times the hyperedge cosine). The similarity floor τ\tau discards weak matches, the advantage-weighted RRF score ranks the survivors, and the capacity cap NmaxN_{\max} keeps the top ones. If no candidate survives, no retrieved skill is injected. The protocol skill of C1, when enabled for the dataset, is injected for every question regardless of the gate.

Complexity Analysis. Per query, retrieval is one exact (brute-force) cosine search at 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|+|ℰ|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|\!+\!|\mathcal{E}|), both gates are linear in the candidate pool, and the prompt grows by at most NmaxN_{\max} skills.

C3: Execution Protocol. Every rollout runs the agent loop of §3.3 with the dataset’s C3 options: the prompt carries the injected context, the question, and the suffix and evidence texts of Prompts P12–P13; tool calls are parsed strictly or leniently; and a final-answer turn (P11) closes rollouts without an answer. With self-consistency, ksck_{\mathrm{sc}} samples vote by plurality (greedy answer on a tie).

End-to-end pipeline. In every training batch, Algorithm 3 with the training settings feeds the rollouts of Algorithm 1, whose admissions and rewards drive Algorithm 2; at evaluation the library is frozen and Algorithms 3 and 4 serve each test question. The nested ablations of Figure 4 (w/o C2 contains w/o C1; w/o C3 stands alone) act at evaluation on the trained library (Appendix E.5).

Appendix D Benchmark Details

This appendix expands §4.1 into a reference for HyperSkill-Bench, which curates 1111 public datasets, with no new data, into one training-free skill-evolution benchmark with a unified JSONL schema. §D.1 covers the sourcing and §D.2 the evaluation; qq, a∗a^{*} and m∈ℳm\!\in\!\mathcal{M} are as in §3.

D.1 Dataset Details

We collect 1111 public datasets, group them into four regimes by dominant modality, and convert every sample into a unified JSONL record rec⁡(s)=(q,a∗,m,task_type,resource_type,assets)\mathrm{rec}(s)\!=\!(q,a^{*},m,\text{task\_type},\text{resource\_type},\text{assets}) where assets stores the relative paths of any images, PDFs, video or audio referenced by qq; we sample 128128 training questions per dataset (deduplicated by exact question text, seed 4242; for AIME2024/2025 from DAPO-Math [52] and for WebWalkerQA from AFM-RL [22]) and evaluate on 3030 test questions for AIME2024/2025 and 6464 for each of the other nine datasets (636636 questions in total).

Text reasoning. AIME2024 and AIME2025 [29, 30] are the canonical math-reasoning probes used by RL-trained reasoners [14, 49]; resources are empty and answers are integers. WebWalkerQA [45] contributes open-web agent QA; as on VL-Web, every method answers it through the text_search tool (§4.1), which gemini-3.8-flash serves as a knowledge source in place of live web search.

VL-Web (web-search VQA). FVQA [46], InfoSeek [4], SimpleVQA [5] and LiveVQA [12] pair an image IqI_{q} with a question whose answer requires entity-level web evidence; the four datasets stress different difficulty axes: FVQA on factual visual knowledge, InfoSeek on long-tail entities, SimpleVQA on everyday recognition, and LiveVQA on recent, time-sensitive events.

VL-Doc (long-document QA). DocBench [59] and MMLongBench-Doc [27] pair a multi-page PDF with a question grounded in a small number of pages; resources are PDF paths, and a per-document BM25 chunk index is built once and shared by every method; search is restricted to the question’s own PDF, and image-only PDFs of MMLongBench-Doc are indexed through local OCR. Score differences on VL-Doc therefore reflect how each method uses this shared index.

Omni (audio-video reasoning). OmniVideoBench [21] pairs a video with a question whose answer requires temporal grounding across visual frames, while WorldSense [16] pairs a video clip and its audio track with a question that requires fusing visual and acoustic cues, delivered as 3232 uniformly sampled keyframes plus the dataset’s audio track (extracted with ffmpeg when missing) in one call; OmniVideoBench questions receive 88 keyframes. The same frame counts apply to every method.

D.2 Evaluation Details

All metrics are percentages. Let tok⁡(⋅)\mathrm{tok}(\cdot) denote whitespace tokenisation after lowercasing and removing punctuation and articles; the answer-shape branch follows the released evaluator.

Token-level F1F_{1} (primary). The prediction a^\hat{a} is the content of the last <answer> tag, or the whole response if there is none. Token-F1F_{1} with answer-shape awareness applies option-letter matching when a∗a^{*} is an option letter, substring or token-set containment when a∗a^{*} is a short entity of at most 55 tokens, and SQuAD-style token-F1F_{1} otherwise. The main table uses a CJK-aware tokeniser that splits Chinese, Japanese and Korean text into single characters and otherwise splits at whitespace: F1​(a^,a∗)=2​|tok⁡(a^)∩tok⁡(a∗)|/(|tok⁡(a^)|+|tok⁡(a∗)|)F_{1}(\hat{a},a^{*})\!=\!2|\mathrm{tok}(\hat{a})\!\cap\!\mathrm{tok}(a^{*})|/(|\mathrm{tok}(\hat{a})|\!+\!|\mathrm{tok}(a^{*})|), reported as RF1=⋅F1\mathrm{R}_{F_{1}}\!=\!100\!\cdot\!F_{1}.

Exact Match and format score. Neither is reported. On AIME the gold is a short integer, and the containment rule above applies to the answer tag, or to the full response without a tag, for every column. The format score (final answer inside an <answer> tag) is logged in training only.

Reward and reported statistic. The GRPO advantage of §3.2 is computed against the token-F1F_{1} reward r=F1​(a^,a∗)r\!=\!F_{1}(\hat{a},a^{*}) alone (whitespace tokeniser; Table 2 uses the CJK-aware variant). Every cell of Table 2 and Figure 4 is the full-set mean of the per-question F1F_{1} from a single evaluation run; a rollout with a provider error scores 00, as for two OmniVideoBench questions in every column. Differences are tested with a paired bootstrap over questions (1010k resamples). HyperSkill’s margins over the best other column have 95% intervals of [−4.1,+8.3][-4.1,+8.3] on WebWalkerQA, [−2.3,+10.0][-2.3,+10.0] on SimpleVQA, [−7.3,+9.8][-7.3,+9.8] on LiveVQA, [−4.3,+13.0][-4.3,+13.0] on DocBench and [−6.3,+15.0][-6.3,+15.0] on WorldSense. Re-running HyperSkill with a freshly trained library changed the 11-dataset average by +0.08+0.08 (95% interval [−1.38,+1.54][-1.38,+1.54]) and single datasets by up to 3.23.2 points (SimpleVQA).

Appendix E Baseline Details

This appendix expands Table 1 into a per-method specification: for Zero-shot and the 66 training-free baselines, the 33 HyperSkill ablations, and HyperSkill itself, we report (i) Overview (purpose and substrate), (ii) Per-task implementation (admission/retrieval/update) and (iii) Hyperparameters. Methods are grouped into Zero-shot and three paradigm classes (§E.1–§E.4), followed by the ablations (§E.5) and HyperSkill (§E.6). Throughout we reuse πθ\pi_{\theta} (frozen gemini-2.5-flash-lite), ff (shared query/skill encoder), Top​-​k​⟨⋅,⋅⟩\mathrm{Top}\text{-}k\!\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle (cosine top-kk), and the reward rr of §D.2; every method shares this backbone, embedder and tool stack. Each baseline builds its own library from the same 128128 training questions with a re-implementation of its published procedure, using the backbone for every LLM call; the baselines retrieve by cosine without a similarity floor and do not receive C3.

E.1 Zero-shot Baseline

Zero-shot [54]. (i) Overview. Bare frozen LLM with task-specific tools and no skill library: every question is answered from πθ(⋅∣q,m)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!q,m). Substrate: empty ℋ=(∅,∅,w)\mathcal{H}\!=\!(\emptyset,\emptyset,w). (ii) Per-task implementation. The agent may call the regime’s tool (text_search on WebWalkerQA and VL-Web, BM25 on VL-Doc; Omni receives keyframes, plus audio on WorldSense) and writes the final answer inside <answer>...</answer>; admission, advantage update, and gating are all unsupported. (iii) Hyperparameters. At most 33 (Text), 55 (VL) or 88 (Omni) rounds and 22 tool calls; greedy decoding at temperature 00 with 10241024 new tokens (20482048 on AIME2025, 40964096 on WorldSense).

E.2 Trajectory-Level Skill Pools

TrainingFreeGRPO [2]. (i) Overview. Replaces gradient updates with an LLM-curated experience pool ℒ={xi}\mathcal{L}\!=\!\{x_{i}\} that distils group-relative semantic advantage from each rollout group and injects retrieved experiences as token-prior hints. Substrate: flat pool indexed by ff. (ii) Implementation in our protocol. Builds its own experience pool from on-policy groups of n=2n\!=\!2 rollouts under the evolving pool (1 epoch, batches of 44): for partially correct groups, each rollout is summarised, a group-advantage call extracts at most one semantic experience, and group and batch update calls apply ADD/UPDATE/DELETE operations. The top experiences by cosine are injected as [<id>]. <experience> (Appendix A). (iii) Hyperparameters. top-k=10k\!=\!10; rollout temperature of run R1.

EvoSkill [1]. (i) Overview. Maintains a Pareto frontier of structured skill folders, each created by failure-driven proposal and retained only if it beats the held-out median. Substrate: ℒfrt={si:gi≥med⁡(g)}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{frt}}\!=\!\{s_{i}:g_{i}\!\geq\!\mathrm{med}(g)\} with one validated gain gig_{i} per skill. (ii) Implementation in our protocol. Runs 33 failure-driven iterations: a proposer sees 88 failed training questions and the current skills and proposes one skill (name, description, at most 55 instructions); the candidate program is kept only if its greedy F1 on 1616 held-out training questions does not drop. The final program’s top skills are injected as > [frontier-skill, val_gain=<gain>] <name>: <description> with numbered instructions. (iii) Hyperparameters. top-k=3k\!=\!3; 33 iterations of 88 failed questions each.

E.3 Code/Card Skill Caches

SkillCraft [3]. (i) Overview. Auto-composes atomic tools into reusable Skills cached as Python-style def si​(⋅)s_{i}(\cdot) snippets, with cache-hit retrieval and no quality ranking. Substrate: code cache ℒ={𝚍𝚎𝚏​si​(⋅)}\mathcal{L}\!=\!\{\,\mathtt{def}\,s_{i}(\cdot)\}. (ii) Implementation in our protocol. Composes each question’s best successful trajectory (reward ≥0.5\geq\!0.5) into one Python-style function over the agent’s atomic operations; a skill is cached only if it parses as one documented function, and a name or docstring match (cosine ≥0.90\geq\!0.90) counts as a cache hit. The top skills are injected as a python code block. (iii) Hyperparameters. top-k=3k\!=\!3; success threshold 0.50.5, cache-hit cosine 0.900.90 and one composition call per success.

AutoSkill [50]. (i) Overview. Distils skills from interaction traces into standardised cards (name + tip) and injects the top matches into future requests for lifelong personalisation. Substrate: tip-card store ℒ={cardi}\mathcal{L}\!=\!\{\mathrm{card}_{i}\} with no per-card quality. (ii) Implementation in our protocol. Extracts a card (name, description, at most 33 tips) from each question’s best successful trace and inserts it, merging it by an LLM call with the nearest card when their cosine is at least 0.850.85. The top cards are injected as * Skill: <name> -- <description> with * Tip: bullets. (iii) Hyperparameters. top-k=3k\!=\!3; merge threshold 0.850.85; at most 33 tips per card and one merge call per near-duplicate.

E.4 Memory-Stream Skills

Memento-Skills [56]. (i) Overview. Stores reusable skills as Markdown files in a stateful memory and selects them through a read/write reflective router conditioned on the current prompt. Substrate: Markdown memory ℒ={mimd}\mathcal{L}\!=\!\{m_{i}^{\mathrm{md}}\} plus a behaviour-trainable router. (ii) Implementation in our protocol. Processes the training cases in order: a top-11 cosine router reads the most similar Markdown skill file, and one reflective call rewrites it, adds a new file, or does nothing. At test time the routed file is injected after [Memory 1] Recall a similar past case:. (iii) Hyperparameters. top-k=1k\!=\!1; the behaviour-trained router is approximated by cosine; one reflective call per case.

XSkill [17]. (i) Overview. Dual-stream framework that distils experiences for tool selection and skills for task orchestration, both grounded in visual observations and merged via cross-rollout critique. Substrate: dual stream {𝒳exp,ℒskill}\{\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{exp}},\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{skill}}\} jointly indexed by ff. (ii) Implementation in our protocol. For every training question, one critique call compares the two rollouts, grounded by a backbone-generated image caption, and outputs at most 22 experiences (“When <condition>, <action>”) and one workflow skill; near-duplicates are dropped. The query embedding f⁡(q,I)f(q,I) averages the text embedding with the embedding of the image caption; the top experiences and the top skill are injected after <> Cross-task experiences: and <> Skill (<name>):. (iii) Hyperparameters. top-33 experiences and top-11 skill; retrieval queries the whole question, not its sub-tasks.

E.5 HyperSkill Ablations

The ablation w/o C2 contains w/o C1, and w/o C3 is applied on its own; all three act at evaluation on HyperSkill’s trained library and keep every other setting of the dataset’s configuration (Appendix E.7); none of them retrains the library or re-tunes a setting specifically for the ablated system.

w/o C1. (i) Overview. HyperSkill without the knowledge distilled in training. This row drops the retrieved skills and replaces the learned protocol skill by one generic text used for every dataset, without re-injection. (ii) Per-task implementation. The floor admits no skill (τ=9\tau\!=\!9); hub correction, P7, the schema-constrained hint and the answer-form line are off. Where the configuration enables the protocol skill, the context is “Output protocol: Answer the question. If tools are available, call them using the tool formats described above. End your response with your final answer inside <answer>...</answer>.” (iii) Hyperparameters. C3 options are left unchanged.

w/o C2. (i) Overview. HyperSkill without test-time delivery: nothing from the library is injected. (ii) Per-task implementation. As w/o C1, and the protocol skill is also off. On AIME2025, WebWalkerQA and MMLongBench-Doc, whose configurations use neither retrieved skills nor the protocol skill, w/o C1 and w/o C2 are identical. (iii) Hyperparameters. C3 options unchanged.

w/o C3. (i) Overview. HyperSkill without the execution protocol. (ii) Per-task implementation. The C3 options are reset to their defaults: no concrete tool prompt, final-answer turn, answer suffix, lenient parser, voting, located pages, question pre-search, time grounding or option check, and the default token budget (10241024 new tokens; 40964096 and 3232 frames on WorldSense), prompt-length limit and round and tool limits. (iii) Hyperparameters. C1, C2 and the library unchanged.

E.6 HyperSkill

HyperSkill. (i) Overview. Counterfactual step-level distillation (C1, §3.1) admits failure-rescuing skills and learns the protocol skill; retrieval feedback updates each skill’s advantage and grows hyperedges (§3.2); an advantage-weighted RRF retriever with similarity/capacity gates and a zero-skill fallback (C2, §3.2) injects only confident matches; and the execution protocol (C3, §3.3) runs the test rollout. Substrate: weighted hypergraph ℋ=(𝒱,ℰ,w)\mathcal{H}\!=\!(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},w) with ui∈[−1,1]u_{i}\!\in\![-1,1]. (ii) Per-task implementation. Each batch applies Eqs. (2)–(3) for admission, Eqs. (4)–(5) for evolution, and Eqs. (6)–(7) for retrieval; evaluation adds the C3 options of the dataset. (iii) Hyperparameters. Defaults of §3, protocol threshold 22 and the per-dataset settings of Appendix E.7.

E.7 Per-Dataset HyperSkill Configuration

Library runs. The three library runs all train for one epoch on the same 128128 training questions with n=2n\!=\!2, batch size 44 and seed 11: R1 uses temperature 0.70.7 (Text) / 1.01.0 (VL, Omni), early stopping, a training-time floor of 0.20.2, and two counterfactual votes on the candidate’s single failed rollout that must both return YES; R2 uses temperature 0.40.4, no early stopping, P7 hints during training rollouts, KeffK_{\mathrm{eff}} probed own failures, and a training-time floor of 0.550.55; R3 equals R2 with a training-time floor of 0.20.2. On AIME2024/2025, WebWalkerQA, FVQA and OmniVideoBench training rollouts also use the concrete tool prompt, final-answer turn, answer suffix and lenient parser, with 81928192 (AIME) or 40964096 tokens; the protocol statistics classify each rollout before its final-answer turn.

Counterfactual probes. Runs R2/R3 probe Keff=min⁡(K,|𝒪q−|)K_{\mathrm{eff}}\!=\!\min(K,|\mathcal{O}_{q}^{-}|) distinct failures of the candidate’s own question and take the strict majority of Eq. (3) over KeffK_{\mathrm{eff}}; with n=2n\!=\!2, a question that yields candidates has exactly one failed rollout (alignment needs a success and a failure), so Keff=1K_{\mathrm{eff}}\!=\!1. Admitted skills enter the library with ui=0.3u_{i}\!=\!0.3, after which only the EMA of Eq. (4) changes uiu_{i}.

Similarity floor. The floor τ\tau of Eq. (7) is set per dataset. Test question-skill cosines of ff lie in [0.31,0.80][0.31,0.80], so a floor of 0.20.2 keeps every candidate and τ=9\tau\!=\!9 admits none. Retrieved skills are injected on InfoSeek (hub-corrected τ~=−0.02\tilde{\tau}\!=\!-0.02), SimpleVQA (τ=0.2\tau\!=\!0.2) and OmniVideoBench (τ=0.55\tau\!=\!0.55). Elsewhere τ=9\tau\!=\!9, and C1’s protocol skill and C3 carry the library’s knowledge.

Injection variants. Retrieved skills are injected through the strategy hint of prompt P7 (Appendix A) or, when P7 is off, as a terse “name: description” list. Three optional variants act only on this injection step: (i) a hub-corrected similarity s~​(q,vi)=⟨f⁡(q),f⁡(vi)⟩−μi\tilde{s}(q,v_{i})\!=\!\langle f(q),f(v_{i})\rangle\!-\!\mu_{i}, where μi\mu_{i} is the mean similarity of viv_{i} to the training questions, used for ranking and for the floor of Eq. (7) so that skills uniformly similar to every query no longer pass the gate; (ii) a schema-constrained hint: P7 must preserve the output schema and, in tool regimes, the tool budget; and (iii) an answer-form line, derived for each skill from the gold answers of its 55 nearest training questions (option letter, short phrase, or free form), followed in tool regimes by the tool budget (see the per-dataset configuration table below).

Appendix F Future Work

HyperSkill improves a frozen backbone by editing an auditable skill library instead of its weights, which leads to four future directions. First, the library can be paired with lightweight parameter updates, e.g. a low-rank adapter that complements the in-context skills. Second, because skills are plain text with an advantage, the libraries of related datasets, such as the four VL-Web datasets that share the text_search tool, can be merged and re-weighted by the EMA of Eq. (4) from new rollouts. Third, C3 refers to tools only through their tags, so extending it to code execution or GUI actions mainly requires new tool tags, budgets and evidence texts, while C1 and C2 stay unchanged. Finally, batched or importance-sampled counterfactual probes can lower the admission cost of C1.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The claims in the abstract and §1 match Table 2, Figure 4 and §4.2.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: We discuss limitations here: each skill library incurs a one-time API cost before serving; counterfactual probes add verification calls at training time; and all experiments use one frozen backbone, with lightweight parameter updates left to future work.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: Propositions 1–3 are in §3; their assumptions and full proofs are in App. B.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Settings: §4.1, §3.3, App. E.7; pseudocode: App. C; prompts: App. A.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: Code and data are public at the URL in the title-page footnote.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: Data splits, tools and decoding are in §4.1, App. D.1 and App. E.7.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: Paired bootstrap 95% intervals (1010k resamples) are in App. D.2.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: API calls only, no GPU (one CPU host); §4.7 reports the API costs.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: We use only licensed public datasets and collect no human-subject data.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: Positive: auditable skill libraries can reduce compute and make agent behaviour editable. Risks: wrong or biased skills could propagate at serving time. Mitigation: we use only public datasets and APIs, and recommend reviewing libraries before deployment.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: Only a pipeline, a public-data benchmark and skill libraries are released.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: All assets are cited (§4.1, App. D) and used under their licences.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: HyperSkill-Bench and the pipeline are documented in App. D, C and A.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: The paper involves no crowdsourcing and no research with human subjects.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: No human subjects are involved, so no IRB approval was required.

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

  76. 16.

    Declaration of LLM usage

  77. Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.

  78. Answer: [Yes]

  79. Justification: The frozen LLM backbone is a core component of the method (App. A).

  80. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components.

    • •

      Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
